notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes below. Some gaps first:

- **Missing sources.** I didn't get NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, any Orthodox page (oca.org), catholic.com, or any page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this psalm. Those are left out. The only Catholic-tradition source I found is Augustine (newadvent.org).
- **Little real disagreement.** I found no verse where Protestant traditions actually disagree. What I did find are different emphases, each from a named teacher: Gill (Baptist), Clarke (Wesleyan), Calvin (Reformed), Luther (cited by another writer), Coffman (Restoration Movement) and Smith (Calvary Chapel). I've marked these as "Emphases."
- **Unclear authors on Bible Hub.** Bible Hub's combined pages sometimes run several commentators together. Where a page didn't show who wrote a line, I've said so.

---

**Introduction**
- The psalm is an acrostic. Apart from the opening "Hallelujah," each of its 22 lines starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Boice (quoted by Guzik) calls Psalms 111 and 112 a matched pair: one about God, the other about the godly person. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-111/ and https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-111.cfm
- Constable thinks the acrostic was meant to help Israelites memorise and recite the psalm. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/111-2.html

**v. 1**
- Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary say "Hallelujah" is not really part of the psalm. It works more like a heading. https://biblehub.com/psalms/111-1.htm
- Bible.org agrees the first line acts as a title, so the acrostic starts at 1b. It suggests "council" and "assembly" may mean two groups: a circle of leaders and the larger crowd of worshippers. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-111
- A sermon on Bible Hub reads the "upright" as like-minded believers and the "congregation" as including people who were indifferent. Its point is that the psalmist praises God in both settings. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/111-1.htm
- *Catholic (Augustine):* the word "confession" here means praising God, not confessing sins. One kind of confession shows the wound to the doctor; the other gives thanks for being healed. He links the "council of the upright" to those who will sit on the twelve thrones. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801111.htm

**v. 2**
- Barnes: God's works are great in number, size, wisdom and goodness. He says it is a mistake for believers to neglect studying God's works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-2.htm
- An unattributed writer on the same page (Guzik quotes the line as from Spurgeon): even God's small works are great. Studying them slowly trains our spiritual sight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-2.htm
- *Commentators disagree on what "works" means.* The Pulpit Commentary says it means God's acts in providence, not the physical creation. Guzik puts the emphasis on creation. The Cambridge Bible says the psalmist means God's acts for Israel, but for Christians it also covers nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-2.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-111/
- *Emphases:* Gill (Baptist) includes creation, providence, Christ's miracles, redemption and God's work of grace in the heart. Calvin (Reformed) says the psalmist later narrows the theme to how God governs the Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-2.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/111-2.html

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew literally says "honour and glory." His "righteousness" means God deals fairly with everything he has made. An unattributed note on the page adds that with God, power and right are never split apart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-3.htm
- Bible.org: the phrase "his righteousness endures forever" links this psalm to Psalm 112. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-111
- Another note on the same page (in MacLaren's style) says Psalms 111 and 112 deliberately mirror each other. God's righteousness and compassion are copied in the godly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-3.htm
- *Emphasis:* Gill (Baptist) applies this to the everlasting righteousness of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-3.htm
- *Catholic (Augustine):* the most glorious of God's works is making the ungodly righteous (justifying them). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801111.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott and Pulpit: the Hebrew literally says "he made a memorial for his wonders." Pulpit thinks remembrance festivals like the Passover are only lightly hinted at. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-4.htm
- The Cambridge Bible links this to the Exodus being passed down the generations, and to the Passover. It also gives a second translation: God made himself a name by his wonders. It traces "gracious and compassionate" back to Exodus 34:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-4.htm
- Barnes: God's works are made to be remembered, and human memory is made to hold on to them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-4.htm
- *Emphases:* Gill (Baptist) lists the Passover, the jar of manna, and the Lord's Supper as memorials of redemption. Clarke (Wesleyan) suggests the psalm may celebrate the return from exile in Babylon. Smith (Calvary Chapel) says this verse refutes the idea that the Old Testament God has no love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-4.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/111-4.html

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: the sense is past tense, "He gave." The Cambridge Bible says the Exodus proved God remembered his covenant with the patriarchs, and promised he always would. The Geneva Bible notes take the "food" as everything his people needed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-5.htm
- *Emphasis:* Coffman (Restoration Movement) connects the "food" with the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/111-4.html
- *Lutheran, Catholic and others (through Delitzsch's commentary, on the v. 4 page):* Delitzsch also ties the food to the Exodus and the Passover meal. He reports that Luther thought the psalm seemed written for Easter. He adds that since Theodoret and Augustine, Christians have linked v. 5 with the Eucharist, and the psalm came to be used at the Lord's Supper. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-4.htm

**v. 6**
- Barnes: God showed his power by what he did, destroying the Egyptians and defeating the peoples of Canaan. Poole: the "heritage" is Canaan. Pulpit prefers the translation "in giving them." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-6.htm
- The Cambridge Bible sees the gift of Canaan as a pledge of a wider rule that would only come true spiritually. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-6.htm
- *Emphasis:* Gill (Baptist) applies the verse to the gospel winning the Gentile world, giving the time of Constantine as an example. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-6.htm
- *Catholic (Augustine):* the "heritage of the nations" was won through martyrs. They passed like camels through the eye of a needle by suffering. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801111.htm

**v. 7**
- The Cambridge Bible: Canaan was given to keep God's promise to the patriarchs, and its people were driven out as just punishment for their sins (Deut 9:4–5). The word "precepts" is found only in the Psalms, and the verse echoes Psalm 19:7–9. The movement from the Exodus to the commandments follows Israel's memory from Egypt to Sinai. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-7.htm
- Barnes: God never acts to support wrong. Allowing people to do evil does not mean he approves of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-7.htm
- *Emphasis:* Gill (Baptist) says Christ has fulfilled all the commandments, and they remain a guide for how we live. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-7.htm
- *Catholic (Augustine):* he applies the verse to martyrs judged by men. He adds that God's promises should not be expected in this life. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801111.htm

**v. 8**
- The Cambridge Bible: to fit the acrostic, the poet uses a word meaning "enacted" rather than its usual sense, "performed." Poole: the precepts rest on truth and uprightness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-8.htm
- *Emphasis:* Gill (Baptist) applies "stand fast forever" to both law and gospel. Faith does not cancel the law, and the gospel is everlasting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: the redemption from Egypt is probably what the writer has in mind, though other rescues may be included. God's name is holy in itself, and so it is to be revered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-9.htm
- Guzik also sees the Exodus behind the verse, framed within God's covenant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-111.cfm
- An unattributed note on Bible Hub says the rescue from Egypt was a picture of the greater redemption Jesus would bring. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-5.htm
- *Catholic (Augustine):* the redemption is from the captivity of our earthly pilgrimage. The covenant is the New Covenant, so readers should not hope for earthly lands and wealth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801111.htm

**v. 10**
- Barnes: "fear" comes from the same root as "reverend" in v. 9. No wisdom is true unless it takes God's claims seriously. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-10.htm
- Spurgeon: "beginning" can also mean "chief." He says obeying God is the test of real wisdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-10.htm
- Gill: this fear is not dread of God's judgments. It is reverent love that is afraid of offending so good a God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-10.htm
- *How to read the last line:* Benson and Gill note it could mean "*its* praise" (the praise of the wise person) rather than God's praise. Spurgeon mentions that reading too. The Cambridge Bible takes it as God's praise, which brings the psalm back to its opening Hallelujah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/111-10.htm
- *Catholic (Augustine):* understanding without doing is dangerous. The praise that lasts forever belongs to God, and it is the believer's final reward and home. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801111.htm
